text: Okay, Council, we are live. We have Mr. Bonifero with us, with Mr. Brewer, and we're going to deal with the PUC matter, I think, early on in the agenda. I want to thank them for attending. First thing I wanted to acknowledge is how well we've done as a community through COVID. And I don't want to acknowledge that to suggest that we should let up. To the contrary, I want to acknowledge it to encourage our community to keep on doing what we've done that put us in the position that we're currently in. We're one of the lowest, I think, the lowest prevalences per 100,000 people in the province of Ontario. Oglum is one of the safest places to be, and Sioux State and Reece, certainly, one of the safest communities to be in. And that's because a lot of us, I think the majority of us, have followed public health advice. And it's not time to stop doing the things that we've done to get us to this position. So as we open up as a community, I want to really encourage people to be mindful of a few simple rules. If you have any COVID-19 symptoms, stay home and self-isolate. So if you're not feeling right, don't go to work, don't go to the store, don't be out and about. If you have any symptoms, stay home and self-isolate. If you don't have symptoms and you're out and about in the community, make sure that you keep a physical distance between you and anybody else of two meters. If you can't do that, we ask that you wear a non-medical mask. At all times, wash your hands. COVID-19 does not stand up to soap and water, so wash your hands when you leave your house, wash your hands when you get home, and wash your hand any time in between that you get a chance to do that. And one of the other things that Algoa Public Health is asking us to do is they're asking us to keep track of who we interact with. And they're doing that so that if you do test positive for COVID-19, then they can contact, trace very quickly, and get in touch with anybody that you may have been in touch with. So, good job to date to St. Marie and Algoma, but let's keep on following these rules as we move forward so we can keep on keeping our community safe. The second point I want to make and the issue I want to raise does relate to community safety. Throughout the COVID-19 crisis, we've seen some systems in place that aren't adequate to deal with the problems that they have. One of those systems is our substance abuse system. And we have seen over the last number of weeks what appears to be an increase in what is publicly termed overdose. So we have seen an increase in people that may be dying from overdoses. But I think that that is somewhat misleading language because when people hear about overdoses, they often think that maybe people consume too much of a drug. And that is the traditional understanding of what an overdose is. But we don't believe that might be what's happening here. What's happening here is people are consuming the substance in the same quantities that they generally do, but the substance is poisoned. And that's the point I think that we need to be mindful of as a community and we need to talk about. Many of us have people in our lives that have substance abuse issues. And just as it's happening across the community and across the province, it can happen to people that we know. So anybody that you do know that has substance abuse issues, talk to them. Talk to them about their substance use and talk to them about the fact that the drug supply is tainted and it's poisoned. And somebody can be consuming a regular amount that they're used to consuming. And that substance use, though unintended, could lead obviously to death. And that really has demonstrated a significant need in this community for more resources and more infrastructure. It's not justifiable that we have the withdrawal management facilities that we currently have. As a matter of fact, we are currently lacking withdrawal management to a large degree. And it has to be addressed. And our frontline workers in this community who are working very hard on a day-to-day basis do not have the resources they need to support the community the way it needs support. So we'll be lobbying our provincial government to address our frankly lack of infrastructure for withdrawal management. And I'd ask the community to join us in that and assist us with it. Because it's hit a critical point and we can't wait any longer to address this issue. And we're seeing the consequence of that through COVID. But back to my original point, I'd ask everybody in our community who knows people who have substance use challenges to talk to them and to make sure they're aware that there's a higher risk and a higher danger right now for fatalities. text: Okay, so we, with all First Nations, we work in three different ways. There's three different programs.
